faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars in orbit around each other. When the orbital plane aligns with our line of sight, one star periodically passes in front of the other, blocking some of its light. This creates a repeating dip in the combined brightness we measure from Earth. By studying these dips, astronomers can learn about the stars' sizes, masses, and orbital properties.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?

faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is a star whose light curve shows the statistical signature of an eclipsing binary but has not yet been checked for contamination from nearby stars. A 'confirmed' candidate is one that passed the automated pixel-level check, meaning the eclipse signal comes from the target star itself, not from light blending in from its neighbors. 'Confirmed' here means it passed this project's vetting pipeline—not that it has been independently verified by other observers or published in scientific journals.
faqs.question: What does 'candidate' mean here, and how is it different from 'confirmed'?

faqs.answer: The ML model is a second opinion on candidate quality. It was trained on 2,274 labeled examples and outperforms the rule-based baseline pipeline. However, it does not gate or filter which candidates get checked. Every candidate that passes statistical and novelty checks still proceeds to the pixel-level check regardless of the ML score. The model is provided as an additional metric for reference only.
faqs.question: What is the machine-learning screening score?

faqs.answer: The pixel-level check is a fully automated analysis of TESS imaging data. It examines whether the eclipse signal originates from the target star or from nearby stars whose light may have blended into the measurement. By comparing the light profile at the target location to nearby pixels and known point-spread functions, the check rejects false positives caused by contamination. No human visual inspection is involved in this process.
faqs.question: How does the pixel-level check work?

faqs.answer: If a period appears potentially aliased, an automated odd/even eclipse-depth test is applied. This compares the brightness dips of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered ones. If the two sets differ significantly, it suggests the measured period may be a harmonic or sub-harmonic of the true period. Such cases are flagged on the individual candidate page so users can understand the caveat.
faqs.question: What if the orbital period looks aliased?

faqs.answer: Yes. All TESS data are public. You can download light curves and images for any target from the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST). The orbital periods and eclipse depths listed on each candidate page allow you to phase-fold the light curve and inspect the eclipse signature yourself. The pixel-level check details are also documented on each page.
faqs.question: Can I verify these results myself?

faqs.answer: This pipeline stops at the pixel-level confirmation step. Being listed on Star Vetter does not automatically place a candidate into scientific catalogs, trigger follow-up observations, or guarantee future study. The candidate and its parameters are made public for use by the community. Whether researchers pursue further analysis--such as spectroscopy to measure stellar masses or radial velocities--is entirely independent of this project.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on this site?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. Eclipsing binaries are pairs of stars that orbit each other and periodically block each other's light, creating a distinctive dip in brightness. The pipeline starts by sampling targets across the sky, applies statistical checks to reject noise and instrumental artifacts, cross-references six major variable-star catalogs to flag novel candidates, and then performs an automated pixel-level check to rule out light from nearby stars contaminating the signal. Of every hundred candidates that pass these gates, roughly ten correspond to real on-target eclipsing binaries. The results are trustworthy because they rely on multiple independent filters: statistical rigor, novelty screening, and automated imaging analysis. A machine-learning model trained on thousands of labeled examples provides a second opinion on candidate quality, outperforming the baseline rule-based approach. The site currently lists 220 confirmed candidates from 1.8% of the TESS observing area.
